claims.text: Crystal-structure selection in noble metal-based HEA nanoparticles is governed by synchronization of individual metal-precursor decomposition events.
Rapid heating narrows and overlaps the decomposition-temperature windows of the constituent precursors.
Overlapping precursor decomposition causes nearly simultaneous nucleation of all constituent metals.
Nearly simultaneous nucleation kinetically traps a metastable single-phase solid solution.
Slower heating permits precursor decomposition events to occur at different times.
Temporally staggered decomposition allows individual metals or metal clusters to nucleate at different times.
Staggered nucleation leads to phase separation and elemental segregation.
Staggered nucleation alters or reduces control over nanoparticle morphology.
Rapid heating followed by rapid cooling produces uniform, metastable, single-phase noble metal HEA nanoparticles.
Rapid heating produces nanoparticles with controlled morphology.
Reducing the heating-ramp rate at fixed composition and cooling conditions will produce multiphase microstructures.
Reducing the heating-ramp rate will produce observable elemental segregation.
Reducing the heating-ramp rate will produce less-controlled particle morphology.
The proposed mechanism applies when synthesis temperatures are near the precursor-decomposition temperatures in noble metal nanoparticle systems containing more than five components.
At sufficiently high thermal energy, thermodynamic equilibration may override kinetic trapping.
